entry.title: Model Evaluation in Machine Learning: How Do We Know a Model Is Good?
entry.summary: Model Evaluation in Machine Learning: How Do We Know a Model Is Good? Building a machine learning model is only one part of a machine learning project. After training a model, we need to answer an important question: How well does it actually perform on new data? This is where model evaluation becomes important. What Is Model Evaluation? Model evaluation is the process of measuring how well a machine learning model makes predictions. It helps us understand whether a model is performing correctly and whether it can generalize to data it has never seen before. A model that performs extremely well on training data may still perform poorly on new data. This problem is commonly known as overfitting. Proper evaluation helps identify such problems before using the model in a real-world applicatio…

entry.title: One field in the request made our agent 3x cheaper and 8x faster
entry.summary: TL;DR. Reasoning models decide by themselves how long to think if you don't tell them. Our agent didn't — and on hard tasks the model sometimes thought for 14 minutes and 33K tokens in a single step. One field in the request body ("reasoning": {"effort": "low"}) made a task 3x cheaper and 7–8x faster, and it solved more tasks, not fewer: 12 of 12 instead of 6 of 7. The best setting in the end was neither "always low" nor "always high" but "low, and high right after a failing test". Below: how we measured it, the tables, the code, and what it doesn't fix. entry.title: I built a voice-to-recipe tool for a friend who never measures anything
entry.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend* I have a friend who cooks everything by feel. Ask her for a recipe and she says "put some masala, add water till it looks right." Nothing is written down, because she doesn't know the amounts herself. But she can explain a dish out loud really well. So I built Voice2Recipe: you put voice notes in a folder, run one Python script, and get a written recipe book. I told the AI not to invent amounts. If the cook doesn't say how much, it writes "to taste", because I didn't want the tool to put words in my friend's mouth. I tested it with free public domain audio from LibriVox, where a volunteer reads an old cookbook. I did this before asking my friend to trust it with her own recipes.
It works, but it isn't perfect. The AI added a "here's a cleaned recipe" line at the top, spelled the author's name wrong, and wrote "to taste" next to an ingredient that needed a real amount. I used the small 1B model, so a person should always read the recipe before trusting it. What my friend said I haven't shown her the result yet, because I was still fixing mistakes. / Voice2Recipe
It's one Python script with two open models, both running on my laptop: Whisper (through faster-whisper) listens to the audio and writes down the text. Gemma (through Ollama) turns that messy text into a recipe with ingredients, steps and tips. My laptop is low on memory, so the script reads audio in 30 second pieces and uses the small Gemma 3 1B model. A voice note of someone cooking is personal, and I didn't want to upload it to a site I don't control. Since Whisper and Gemma run on my own laptop, the audio never leaves it. It also cost nothing and needed no account. The bigger Gemma model didn't fit in my memory, so I switched to the 1B one by changing a single word in the script. With a closed API I wouldn't have had that choice. Best Use of Gemma

entry.title: Validating Container Numbers from Gate OCR with the ISO 6346 Check Digit
entry.summary: Container depots and terminals increasingly read container numbers with OCR cameras at the gate. OCR is fast, but it is not perfect: a smudged 8 becomes a B, a 0 becomes an O. The good news is that every shipping container number carries its own error check, defined in ISO 6346. You can catch most misreads with a few lines of code before they reach your yard system. A container number like CSQU3054383 has four parts: CSQ - the owner code (3 letters) U - the equipment category (U for freight containers) 305438 - the serial number (6 digits) 3 - the check digit Give each letter a value starting at A = 10, skipping multiples of 11 (so 11, 22 and 33 are never used).
